conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported by strong evidence from a randomized controlled trial (MAP.3) and concludes that the claim is accurate.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **supported by strong evidence**. In the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled MAP.3 (Mammary Prevention 3) trial of 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk for breast cancer, exemestane (25 mg/day) reduced invasive breast cancer incidence by 65% compared with placebo (annual incidence 0.19% vs. 0.55%) over a median follow-up of 35 months, with a favorable adverse-event profile relative to other chemopreventive agents like tamoxifen ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507)). This finding was corroborated by the National Cancer Institute's summary of the same ASCO-presented data ([cancer.gov](https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk)) and further discussed in a critical analysis published in a peer-reviewed journal (PMC), which characterized MAP.3 as offering "a potential new standard for pharmaceutical risk reduction in high-risk postmenopausal women" ([PMC3354700](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/)).

Some caveats remain: the original trial had relatively short follow-up (median 35 months), and effects on longer-term outcomes such as breast-cancer-specific mortality and overall survival were not fully established at that time. Later analyses (e.g., from the Intergroup Exemestane Study, cited via ResearchGate/PubMed) confirmed exemestane "significantly reduces the incidence of breast cancer in 'at-risk' postmenopausal women" but called for continued long-term follow-up regarding bone health and other risks ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23569364/)).

**Bottom line:** The claim is accurate—exemestane reduces breast cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at elevated risk, primarily based on robust Phase III randomized trial evidence (MAP.3), though long-term mortality benefit and safety trade-offs (e.g., bone density loss) warrant ongoing consideration.
